Antidepressants Can Cause Violence and Suicide, Researchers Say
I think this is covered in the medicine warnings, right?
Yes, it usually is. The trouble is that when you are in the sort of state produced as a side effect of the medication you are hardly likely to think out the 'why' of how you feel that way.
You're supposed to read the warnings before you use the drug. If you're willing to take the drug after reading the warnings, the results are your problem.

That's an argument that I'm sure lawyers for drug companies use in the lawsuits. Here's the trick. Every single medication on the market can have side effects, up to and including death in some cases. When these matters are argued out in court several factors come into play. One is the severity of the side effect. Personally I'd prefer death, even by suicide, to being a murderer, but in any case the magnitude is taken into account. Death is worse than a rash or an upset stomach. Whether the side effects can be reversed or how long it lasts is a factor.The second factor taken into account is the frequency of the side effect and whether the pharmaceutical company has provided information about that. Usually they don't aside from vague words such as "occasionally", "rarely"" and so on. The magnitude of the side effect as compared to the condition it (presumably) treats is also factored in. In the courtroom the efficacy of the drug is often also discussed. This is basically never presented on package inserts. It is also something that the average consumer is most likely unaware of even in a general sense. To sum up it's a little more complicated than caveat emptor, and responsibility is a matter of continual legal evolution.
I understand why they list everything. But it still seems like it's a fair warning. If you're willing to take the drug, you're willing to take the risk.

There are other factors that come into play. The average consumer thinks that medication A for condition B will always, or almost always, correct condition B. This is far from the truth. In some cases the efficacy is exactly zero. The consumer makes their choice without 'complete information'. Another factor is comparison of the drug used to other medications on the market. Both in terms of efficacy and dangers. This is something that the consumer is also almost always not knowledgeable about. The usual difference is only cost. "New'" drugs are typically more expensive. They may or may not be better, worse or the same in terms of effectiveness. They may or may not have a totally different side effect profile. The point I want to emphasize is that there are factors in deciding to take a drug or not that are hidden rather than explicit to the consumer. The responsibility of the pharmaceutical companies is always under review in the courts because the reality is complex.
